summary: Help 9-10 year-olds write the probability of an equally-likely event as the part-whole fraction favourable/total (P(6)=1/6, P(heads)=1/2, one of three equally represented colours = 1/3), and translate fluently between a situation, its fraction, and a point on the 0-to-1 scale. The central work is holding the part-WHOLE meaning (favourable out of the TOTAL) against the more intuitive part-part ratio/odds, and attaching the symbol to a magnitude on the scale.
misconceptions: Writing the probability as a part-part ratio/odds (1/5 or 1:5 for one red among six) instead of the part-whole fraction 1/6
Answering with a raw frequency or whole number ('3', or Fischbein & Gazit's '3/4 and 4/3') rather than favourable-over-total
Swapping numerator and denominator — putting the total on top
Applying favourable/total to situations whose outcomes are not equally likely

activities.title: Build the fraction from a bag, and place it on the 0-to-1 line
steps: Fill a bag with coloured counters that are identical apart from colour, which you can see and count, and that will be drawn without looking — e.g. drop in one red among six total.
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction: count the favourable (reds) for the numerator and the WHOLE set (all counters, red included) for the denominator, giving 1/6.
Mark that fraction on a 0-to-1 line (1/6 hugging 0, 1/2 at the middle).
Add more reds and re-count: watch the fraction change and the marker slide up the line together.
Deliberately test the wrong answer: try to make it 1/5 (red to the other five) and re-count the total to see the denominator counts all six counters, not the leftovers.
activities.insight: The denominator is the total number of equally likely outcomes (every counter that could be drawn), not the count of the OTHER outcomes; the fraction has a size you can locate between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Interpret a given fraction: what does each number count?
steps: Look at a fair six-sided die alongside the statement P(rolling a 6) = 1/6.
Say what the 1 stands for (one favourable face) and what the 6 stands for (the total number of equally likely faces).
On a labelled die or bag, tap the favourable outcomes to reveal the numerator, then tap the whole set to reveal the denominator.
Then reveal where that fraction sits on the 0-to-1 scale.
activities.insight: In favourable/total, the numerator counts the outcomes you want and the denominator counts ALL equally likely outcomes; the fraction names a magnitude on the scale.

activities.title: Construct and translate from a fresh situation
steps: Take a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter (5 in total).
Write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, forming favourable-over-total: 3/5.
Mark 3/5 on a 0-to-1 scale (a little above the halfway point).
Then write the probability of NOT red and check what the two fractions add up to.
Try another fair case: a bag with three equally represented colours gives P(one colour) = 1/3, marked a little below the halfway point on the scale.
Reduce a case where it applies: a standard 52-card deck has 26 red cards, so P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2 — connect counting outcomes to equivalent fractions.
activities.insight: Building the fraction from a NEW situation — not reading a prepared one — is where part-whole understanding shows: a part-whole reasoner writes 3/5, a part-part reasoner writes 3/2 or 3:2 (red to non-red).

activities.title: Check the outcomes are equally likely before counting
steps: Before writing favourable/total, ask: are all the outcomes equally likely?
Compare a fair die or a bag of identical counters (equally likely) with an uneven spinner whose regions differ in size (not equally likely).
For the uneven case, notice why counting colours or regions does not directly give the probability.
activities.insight: favourable/total gives the probability only when the outcomes are equally likely; otherwise the counts of colours/regions are not counts of equally likely outcomes.

activities.title: Talk it through: why that number on the bottom?
steps: Answer a prompt such as 'What goes on the bottom of the fraction, and why?'
If you give a part-part answer, re-count the whole set and explain which outcomes the denominator includes.
Using your 3 red, 1 blue, 1 green bag, explain whether adding two more green counters would change the probability of red, and which number in your fraction changes.
activities.insight: Articulating that the denominator counts the whole set of equally likely outcomes consolidates part-whole reasoning.

checkQuestion: Two moves. First INTERPRET: show a fair six-sided die and the written statement 'P(rolling a 6) = 1/6'. Ask the child what the 1 and the 6 each stand for. Then TRANSLATE/CONSTRUCT: hand them a bag holding 3 red, 1 blue and 1 green counter and ask them to write the probability of drawing red as a fraction, and mark it on a 0-to-1 scale. Watch the construction step closely.
checkAnswer: Interpret: the 6 is the total number of equally likely outcomes (the six faces), the 1 is the number of favourable outcomes (one face shows a 6). Construct: P(red) = 3/5 (three red out of five counters altogether), marked a little above the halfway point on the 0-to-1 scale.
